issues.legal_issue: The remaining provisions of an estate-abolition enactment are constitutionally valid where they fall within the constitutional protection for laws relating to the acquisition of estates.
material_facts: The enactment abolished jagirs and provided for resumption of jagir lands and compensation.
A jagirdar challenged the provisions upheld by the Judicial Commissioner, but did not press his appeal in the Supreme Court.
The Court held that the enactment as a whole fell within the protection of Article 31A and relied on earlier decisions concerning similar legislation.
issues.conclusion: The jagirdar’s appeal was dismissed, and the Court upheld the constitutional validity of the rest of the enactment.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31A protects laws providing for the acquisition of estates and provisions incidental to that acquisition. The Court relied on The State of Bihar v. Maharajadhiraja Sir Kameshwar Singh [1952] SCR 889; Visweshwar Rao v. State of Madhya Pradesh [1952] SCR 1020; Raja Suriya Pal Singh v. State of U.P. [1952] SCR 1056; K. C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa [1954] SCR 1; Thakur Amar Singhji v. State of Rajasthan [1955] 2 SCR 303; Raja Bhairebendra Narayan Bhup v. State of Assam [1956] SCR 303; Sri Ram Ram Narain v. State of Bombay [1959] Supp. (1) SCR 499; Raghubir Singh v. State of Ajmer (now Rajasthan) [1959] Supp. (1) SCR 478; and Atma Ram v. State of Punjab [1959] Supp. (1) SCR 748.

predicates.individual_appeal_against_upholding_vali: An individual appealed a decision that had upheld the validity of an enactment.
predicates.estate_abolition_enactment: The enactment provided for abolishing an estate and acquiring or resuming the estate’s land.
predicates.enactment_protected_as_estate_acquisitio: The enactment and its relevant provisions concerned the acquisition of estates and were within the constitutional protection for such laws.

issues.definition: When an individual appeals a decision upholding an estate-abolition enactment that is protected as a law for estate acquisition, the enactment is constitutionally valid.

issues.legal_issue: A legislative scheme that allots land to estate holders after resumption is not invalid as colourable legislation merely because it distinguishes them from other occupants or imposes conditions on allotment, where the legislature is competent and the scheme is within the protection for estate acquisition.
material_facts: The enactment allowed an estate holder to retain certain land after resumption and prescribed how that land would be allotted.
The provision first allotted land personally cultivated continuously for three years before resumption, with further allotment in specified circumstances to reach a minimum area.
Other occupants were treated under a separate provision that deemed them tenants in respect of land recorded as occupied at resumption.
The Court considered estate holders and other occupants to be distinct classes; it also held that even assuming discrimination, the provision was protected by Article 31A.
The provision implemented the enactment’s scheme for acquisition and resumption of estates, and the legislature had authority over the subject under Entry 18 of List II.
issues.conclusion: Section 22(1) was valid and constitutional; it was neither colourable legislation nor invalid discrimination.
issues.legal_principle: Colourable legislation concerns legislative competence, not legislative motive or good faith. The question is whether the legislature, while purporting to act within its powers, has in substance transgressed them under a pretence or disguise; a legislature cannot do indirectly what it cannot do directly. K. C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v. State of Orissa [1954] SCR 1 supplies this principle. The Court held the legislature competent under Entry 18 of List II and held the provision, as part of the estate-acquisition scheme, protected by Article 31A. It also relied on Raghubir Singh v. State of Ajmer (now Rajasthan) [1959] Supp. (1) SCR 478 for protection of provisions incidental to acquisition.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge to_estate_acquisition_law and legislature_competent_over_land and land_allotment_incidental_to_acquisition and (estate_holders_distinct_from_other_occupants or provision_protected_as_estate_acquisition)

predicates.constitutional_challenge: A party challenged the constitutionality of a legislative provision.
predicates.to_estate_acquisition_law: The challenged provision formed part of a law providing for acquisition or resumption of estates.
predicates.legislature_competent_over_land: The legislature had authority to legislate on the subject of land and land rights.
predicates.land_allotment_incidental_to_acquisition: The provision prescribed the land an estate holder could retain or receive as part of the acquisition scheme.
predicates.estate_holders_distinct_from_other_occup: The provision treated estate holders differently from other occupants because they belonged to distinct classes.
predicates.provision_protected_as_estate_acquisitio: The provision fell within the constitutional protection for laws concerning estate acquisition, including provisions incidental to acquisition.

issues.definition: A challenged land-allotment provision in an estate-acquisition law is constitutionally valid when the legislature is competent and the provision is incidental to acquisition, if the classes are distinct or the provision is constitutionally protected.

issues.legal_issue: A competent legislature may expressly bar civil-court jurisdiction over matters assigned to authorities under an enactment without creating repugnancy with the general civil-court jurisdiction rule.
material_facts: The enactment assigned specified matters to revenue and land-reform authorities and expressly barred civil courts from deciding those matters or questioning the authorities’ orders, subject to the enactment’s exceptions.
The Civil Procedure Code gave civil courts jurisdiction over civil suits except where their cognizance was expressly or impliedly barred.
The Court held that the State legislature had authority to legislate on the jurisdiction of courts under Entry 3 of List II.
issues.conclusion: Section 37 was valid and constitutional; it was not repugnant to section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
issues.legal_principle: Section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure grants civil courts jurisdiction over civil suits except those whose cognizance is expressly or impliedly barred. A competent legislature may make such a bar, and section 9 itself recognizes its effect. The State legislature had authority under Entry 3 of List II to legislate on the jurisdiction of courts.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge to_jurisdiction_bar and competent_legislature_over_courts and enactment_assigns_matter_to_authority and enactment_expressly_bars_civil_court

predicates.constitutional_challenge: A party challenged the constitutionality of a legislative provision.
predicates.to_jurisdiction_bar: The challenged provision limited civil courts’ authority to decide certain matters.
predicates.competent_legislature_over_courts: The legislature had authority to legislate on the jurisdiction of courts.
predicates.enactment_assigns_matter_to_authority: The enactment assigned the relevant matter to a designated administrative or specialist authority.
predicates.enactment_expressly_bars_civil_court: The enactment expressly excluded civil-court jurisdiction over the assigned matter.

issues.definition: When a competent legislature assigns a matter to an authority and expressly excludes civil-court jurisdiction over it, the jurisdiction bar is valid.

issues.legal_issue: A compensation method that deducts the value of land retained by an estate holder does not deprive the holder of proprietary interest without compensation where the holder is relieved of the land-revenue burden and that burden is accounted for in computing compensation.
material_facts: The compensation schedule deducted from gross income an amount representing the rent value of land allotted to or retained by an estate holder.
The estate holder would be required to pay rent for that land but would no longer pay the land revenue previously payable on it.
The land revenue was taken into account in determining the net assets used to calculate compensation.
The Court held that the holder retained possession of the land for other purposes and was not deprived of the proprietary interest without compensation.
issues.conclusion: Clause 4(e) of the Schedule was valid and constitutional.
issues.legal_principle: The Court assessed the compensation method in light of the actual financial effect of the deduction: the land-revenue burden ceased, and that revenue was accounted for in arriving at the net assets for compensation. The enactment fell within the protection of Article 31A.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge to_compensation_method and land_retained_by_former_owner and retained_land_rent_value_deducted and former_owner_relieved_of_land_revenue and land_revenue_accounted_for_in_compensation

predicates.constitutional_challenge: A party challenged the constitutionality of a legislative provision.
predicates.to_compensation_method: The challenged provision prescribed how compensation for acquired property was to be calculated.
predicates.land_retained_by_former_owner: The former owner retained possession of some land after the acquisition.
predicates.retained_land_rent_value_deducted: The compensation calculation deducted an amount representing the rent value of the retained land.
predicates.former_owner_relieved_of_land_revenue: The former owner ceased to owe the land revenue previously payable on the retained land.
predicates.land_revenue_accounted_for_in_compensati: The land revenue on the retained land was taken into account in calculating compensation.

issues.definition: A compensation method is constitutionally valid when it deducts the rent value of retained land, the former owner is relieved of land revenue, and that revenue is accounted for in compensation.
